name: breeding_age_min
evidence_or_assumption: Published: no female bred before age 3 (6 known-age females; first breeding at 3 for 3 of them).  Low 2 is the age catsg gives as possible, not observed in this study.  High 4 is chosen by us for sensitivity.

name: breeding_age_max
evidence_or_assumption: Published: last reproduction at age 9 for two females; a third last bred at 8 and left the area at 11.  Range is the observed spread across three females.

name: annual_breeding_probability
area_age_group: females aged 3 to 9, Donana (Coto del Rey)
evidence_or_assumption: Published: 83.3 +/- 5.4% of adult females bred per year over 9 years (yearly range 66.7 to 100); 24 of 29 female-years.  Range is the observed yearly range.  Source subpopulation is protected and has the highest rabbit density in Donana, so this may be an upper value.

name: litter_size_at_birth
area_age_group: litters seen before 4 weeks, Donana (Coto del Rey)
evidence_or_assumption: Published: mean 3.0 +/- 0.16 (n=16 litters), range 2 to 4.  Counted before cubs were 4 weeks old, so it is a minimum number born.  One female raised 5 cubs (mean 3.1, n=17, range 2 to 5).

name: cub_cumulative_survival_3mo
area_age_group: cubs born in Coto del Rey (n=63)
evidence_or_assumption: Published point value 75% (males 73%, females 73%).  Low and high are a Wilson 95% interval computed by us from the published percentage and n; the paper gives no interval.

name: cub_cumulative_survival_10mo
evidence_or_assumption: Published point value 69%.  No death was found between 3 and 10 months; cubs of unknown fate are excluded from n.  Low and high are a Wilson 95% interval computed by us from the published percentage and n; the paper gives no interval.

name: cub_cumulative_survival_to_dispersal
evidence_or_assumption: Published point value 57%.  Four deaths were found between 10 months and dispersal; cubs of unknown fate are excluded from n.  Low and high are a Wilson 95% interval computed by us from the published percentage and n; the paper gives no interval.

name: sex_ratio_female_per_male_at_birth
evidence_or_assumption: Published ratio 1.03:1.00.  Low and high are chosen by us for sensitivity; no interval is published.  The EU report cites biased sex ratios in the declining Donana subpopulation (second-hand).

name: birth_month
evidence_or_assumption: Published: 14 of 16 births in March, one in April, one in June (the June birth followed a lost territory and a pseudopregnancy).  catsg: most births in March and April, gestation about two months, mating January to July.

name: dispersal_age_months
evidence_or_assumption: Published: most lynx dispersed at 12 to 24 months, mostly January to June (24 of 29).  Baseline 18 is the midpoint, chosen by us.  catsg gives a wider 8 to 28 months.  ferreras2004 (full text read 2026-10-25) gives a mean age at start of dispersal of 17.8 +/- 1.2 (SE) months, with 15.4 to 15.5 in Coto del Rey and 19.3 to 20.8 in Reserva Biologica; all dispersers left before 28 months and most between 13 and 24; by 2 years the probability of having dispersed was at least 0.78 for either sex.

name: dispersal_settlement_fraction
evidence_or_assumption: Published (ferreras2004, full text read 2026-10-25): at least 13 of 27 dispersers (48%) settled in a territory; the fate of 7 was unknown, so if those 7 are among the 27 the share lies between 48% and 74% (our arithmetic); females settled more often than males (66.7% against 38.4%, not significant).  Low and high are chosen by us for sensitivity.  Dispersers died at higher rates than non-dispersers of the same age:  annual survival 0.480 (12 to 24 months) and 0.442 (24 to 36 months) against 0.915 and 1.000, and 8 of 11 deaths of dispersers were illegal hunting.  The observed minimum share is 0.48, so the low value of 0.3 is below any observation.

name: annual_mortality_rate_all_causes
area_age_group: radio-tagged lynx, Donana and surroundings, 1983 to 1989
evidence_or_assumption: Published point estimate 0.37 (Heisey-Fuller method; ferreras1992, full text read 2026-10-25):  30 radio-tagged lynx, Donana, 1983 to 1989, a declining population, 95% interval 0.18 to 0.51.  By status the rates were 0.12 (resident males), 0.21 (resident females), 0.00 and 0.31 (young males and females before dispersal), and 0.86 and 0.70 (dispersing males and females), so 0.37 is a mixture that deaths of dispersers dominate.  Low and high are chosen by us for sensitivity.  palomares2005 states that mortality inside the national park is very low, so 0.37 likely overstates a protected subpopulation.  ferreras2004 (full text read 2026-10-25) shows that survival depends strongly on status:  annual survival of 0.915 (12 to 24 months) and 1.000 (24 to 36 months) for lynx that stayed in the natal area against 0.480 and 0.442 for dispersers, in Donana.  One all-cause rate of 0.37 is far above the first (mortality 0.00 to 0.09) and below the second (0.52 to 0.56); the model has no age- or status-specific mortality.

name: death_share_illegal_trapping
area_age_group: radio-tagged lynx, Donana and surroundings, 1983 to 1989
evidence_or_assumption: Published (ferreras1992, full text read 2026-10-25):  41.7% of the annual mortality rate, not of deaths; of all 24 recorded deaths, 8 (33.3%) were illegal trapping.  The percentages of the rate are multiples of 1/12, although the paper's Table 2 lists 11 radio-tagged deaths, so the base is unclear; the interval is a Wilson 95% interval for 5 of 12 (our inference).  This share is already inside annual_mortality_rate_all_causes; do not add it.

name: death_share_road_traffic
area_age_group: radio-tagged lynx, Donana and surroundings, 1983 to 1989
evidence_or_assumption: Published (ferreras1992, full text read 2026-10-25):  16.7% of the annual mortality rate, not of deaths; of all 24 recorded deaths, 5 (20.8%) were road traffic.  Same inference and interval method as above (2 of 12).  Already inside annual_mortality_rate_all_causes; do not add it.

name: female_home_range_km2
evidence_or_assumption: Published average 10 km2 for females in Donana (catsg).  Low and high are the species range for both sexes pooled (4 to 30 km2), so they are wide.  Evidence on food is MIXED:  catsg and palomares2001a (full text read 2026-10-25) say ranges are smaller where rabbits are abundant (across sites), but the palomares2001a result rests on five ranges, with one female range inferred from male ranges; palomares2005 says a rabbit decline did not change home range inside Coto del Rey; lopezbao2014 found exclusive space use did not depend on food.  Treat a food effect on range size as an ASSUMPTION to test, not a measured function.  palomares2001 (read in part 2026-10-24) measured 9.5 km2 for adult females in Donana in 1992 to 1996 and found no link between rabbit density and range size (P above 0.2); lopezbao2014 (accepted manuscript, read in part 2026-10-25) tested overlap between females, not range area, and found low overlap and nearly exclusive cores across a wide rabbit gradient; the two 2001 papers by the same author disagree on that link, and the palomares2001a result is weak (five ranges, strongly correlated predictors, one influential point).

name: female_home_range_overlap_index
area_age_group: resident females, Donana, three decades of data
evidence_or_assumption: Published (abstract): median home range overlap among resident females 0.08 (range 0 to 0.57); core area overlap median 0 (range 0 to 0.22).  Supports modeling one breeding female per territory.  The abstract gives no years or sample size.

name: male_home_range_km2
evidence_or_assumption: Published average 18 km2 for males in Donana.  Low and high as for females (species range, sexes pooled).  Male ranges overlap those of several females.  palomares2001 (read in part 2026-10-24) measured 18.2 km2 for adult males in Donana in 1992 to 1996.

name: diet_rabbit_fraction
evidence_or_assumption: Published: rabbits are 80 to 100% of the diet (catsg) or 80 to 99% (EU report).  Baseline is the midpoint, chosen by us.  Supports using rabbit density as the single food input.

name: rabbit_density_spring_min_for_territorial_breeding
evidence_or_assumption: Published (palomares2001, read in part 2026-10-24):  rabbit densities as low as 1.0 per hectare in autumn and 4.6 in spring, the lowest recorded, were enough to support lynx reproduction in Donana in 1992 to 1996.  The study says it could not determine the minimum density at which lynx fail, or the effect of density on how many females breed.  The EU report reads these figures as densities that are needed; the primary source does not.  The model rule, no breeding below this value, is an ASSUMPTION.  Low 4.0 is the lowest spring density recorded in palomares2005, which the authors say might be close to critical.  High 6.0 is chosen by us.  palomares2001a (full text read 2026-10-25) gives the same two figures as a pellet conversion:  114 pellets per m2 is about 4.6 rabbits per hectare in spring and 1.0 in autumn (it cites an in-press paper that the reference list gives as palomares2001b; we found no such conversion there, so its origin is unverified).  It calls 114 a level at which lynx density may be higher because ranges shrink, and about 80 pellets per m2 (the resident-site mean was 79.7) the level for stable resident areas.  Do not convert pellets to density with this paper:  palomares2001b (full text read 2026-10-25) found that pellet counts predict line-transect density poorly in Mediterranean scrubland (adjusted r2 0.10, P = 0.082, n = 23; 0.43 when edge plots replace scrubland plots).  The threshold sensitivity runs stay at 3.0, 4.6, and 6.0 (docs/model-conventions.md).

name: rabbit_density_autumn_min_for_territorial_breeding
evidence_or_assumption: Published (palomares2001, read in part 2026-10-24):  1.0 per hectare was the lowest autumn density recorded (autumn 1996), and lynx reproduction was not affected.  It is a level that was enough, not a measured minimum.  Unused while the density is constant within a run.  Low and high are chosen by us for sensitivity.

name: food_level_low_rabbits_per_ha
evidence_or_assumption: ASSUMPTION: anchored to the autumn figure (1.0 per hectare, the lowest autumn density recorded in palomares2001), but applied as a spring density, where the lowest recorded was 4.6.  No source tested breeding at 1.0 in spring.  Needs a team decision.

name: food_level_medium_rabbits_per_ha
evidence_or_assumption: ASSUMPTION: anchored to the spring figure (4.6 per hectare, the lowest spring density recorded in palomares2001, at which lynx still reproduced).  Needs a team decision.

name: food_level_high_rabbits_per_ha
evidence_or_assumption: ASSUMPTION: anchored to the highest density recorded in Coto del Rey (range 4 to 55 over the study).  Low 20 is chosen by us.  palomares2005 found no effect of rabbit density on reproduction or cub survival across 4 to 55, so medium and high may give similar results; that would match the evidence.
